metric_rationale: The design was built so that on 12 of the 16 unique pairs (72 of 96 trials per subject) the tallies for A and B differ while the top-validity discriminating cue favors the option with FEWER feature wins — i.e., TTB and Tallying make strictly opposite predictions on every one of these trials (e.g., trial 2: A=[1,0,0,0,0] vs B=[0,1,1,0,0]; TTB picks A via cue 1, Tallying picks B via a 2-vs-1 tally; trial 15: cue 3 favors A but the tally is 1-vs-2 for B). The metric computes, purely from the observed choices, the proportion of these conflict trials on which the subject picked the TTB-favored option. Under TTB-simulated data this equals (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 on every such trial — well above 0.5 for any non-trivial beta, and approaching ~1 for moderate/large beta. Under Tallying-simulated data it equals (1-eps)*(1 - sigmoid(margin*beta)) + eps/2 with margin >= 1 — well below 0.5, approaching ~eps/2 for moderate/large beta. So the two theories produce a large mean gap (typically 0.5-0.9 apart) in opposite directions. Crucially, the metric is a bounded proportion estimated from ~72 Bernoulli trials per subject, so per-subject sampling variance is tiny (<= p(1-p)/72 ~ 0.0035), making the between-subject variance small for both theories; with N=25 human subjects Welch's t-test on the (mean, variance) pairs will separate the theories decisively. The metric is computed generically from the ratings columns (cue cascade + tally counts recomputed row-wise), so it also runs unchanged on a single subject's slice, satisfying the per-subject variance requirement. Unlike a raw 'fit to TTB' measure, it is restricted to the double-dissociation trials where the two theories make opposite deterministic predictions, which is exactly where the design has maximal diagnostic leverage and where noise from the tie-trials (where Tallying guesses) cannot dilute the contrast.

The design's core dissociation is the CONFLICT cell: trials where the tally majority (the designated winner W) is opposed by the highest-validity discriminating cue. On those trials the two theories make opposite-signed predictions about P(choose W) for ANY noise parameters: Tallying gives P(W) = sigmoid(m*beta) with m >= 1, hence strictly > 0.5 (it obeys the cue majority even against the best cue); TTB gives P(W) = 1 - sigmoid(beta), hence strictly < 0.5 (it obeys the single top cue against the majority). So the metric P(W | conflict) - 0.5 is positive under Tallying and negative under TTB regardless of beta, epsilon, or which cue position d decides — the sign itself is diagnostic, and the magnitude grows with beta on both sides (the gap is (1-epsilon)*[weighted sigma(m*beta) + sigma(beta) - 1] over the 64 conflict trials per subject). This uses 64 of 96 trials per subject (conflict base trials 1,2,3,4,7,8,9,11,13,14,15,16,19,20,21,23 x 4 reps), giving tight per-subject estimates: e.g., at beta=1 the Tallying value is ~ +0.31 and the TTB value ~ -0.23 (gap ~0.55) with per-subject SD ~0.05-0.06, which at N=25 yields a Welch t in the dozens; even at the minimum beta=0.1 the gap (~0.07) still exceeds the per-subject noise (~0.018 SE). Congruent trials are deliberately excluded: at m=1 congruent both theories predict exactly sigmoid(beta), so they add variance without adding mean separation. The metric is computed identically on the pooled DataFrame and on single-subject slices (each subject has all 24 unique pairs), so between-subject variance is well defined. The classification (tally winner, top discriminating cue via the fixed descending-validity order) is recomputed from the raw ratings on every row, so no list-column hashing is needed.

The core dissociation: TTB's score is binary (winner=1, loser=0), so its softmax+lapse collapses to ONE constant probability of picking the TTB winner on every non-tied trial — it is completely blind to which cue decides and to what the lower cues say. VWEI instead produces a graded profile: when the 90% expert decides (pairs 1-4, E_rel = +8.6 to +10.6) it picks the TTB winner ~85% of the time, but when cue 2 or cue 3 decides against a weighted opposing coalition (pairs 7-12, 15-16, E_rel = -0.65 to -3.0) it picks the TTB winner only ~35-47% of the time. The metric is the difference in 'pick the TTB winner' rates between these two trial classes. Because it is a within-subject difference of rates, each subject's overall response bias (their beta and epsilon, which under TTB is the ONLY thing that varies) cancels exactly: under TTB the metric is 0 in expectation for every parameter setting; under VWEI it is ~+0.42 (0.85 vs ~0.42 averaged over the 48 low trials). Per subject there are 24 high trials and 48 low trials (6 reps each of the 16 pairs), so the binomial noise of the difference is small (per-subject SD ~0.10-0.13), giving a Welch t at N=25 of roughly 13 — far beyond the alpha=0.01 threshold. The trial classification is structural (computed from the fixed stimulus vectors with gamma=3 weights), so it is deterministic and identical for every subject and for the pooled data; the sign of E_rel for every classified pair is robust across VWEI's entire gamma range [2.8, 3.2], and pairs with ambiguous evidence (pairs 5-6, 13-14) are deliberately excluded from both classes to keep the contrast clean. The metric works identically on a single subject's slice (24/48 trials) and on the pooled DataFrame.

Core logic. On this design TTB's prediction collapses to a single stimulus-invariant constant: its probability of choosing its own winner is q = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 on every one of the 23 pairs (softmax over a binary score never sees anything but the winner identity). VWEI instead predicts P(choose TTB's winner) = sigmoid(beta * x), where x is the VWEI evidence signed toward TTB's winner — I verified this identity trial-by-trial (e.g., trial 1: x=+2.78, P=0.636; trial 8: x=-2.46, P=0.380; trial 15: x=-2.46, P=0.380; trial 19: x=-2.46, P=0.620... wait, trial 19's winner is B with x=-2.46 so P(choose winner)=0.620). So the OLS slope of 'chose TTB's winner' on signed evidence x is exactly 0 under TTB (for ANY beta, epsilon) and clearly positive (~0.049 at gamma=3, beta=0.2, eps=0; still >=0.043 across the full VWEI box gamma in [2.8,3.2], beta in [0.18,0.23], eps in [0,0.03]) under VWEI. The metric needs no trial lookup — x and the TTB winner are recomputed from the raw rating vectors with the design's fixed validities, so it is robust to trial ordering, mirroring, and rep counts. Power analysis: with 92 trials/subject the per-trial x spread gives Sxx ~= 202, so the per-subject slope SD is about sqrt(0.25/202) ~= 0.035 under the noisiest TTB parameterization (q=0.5) and similar under VWEI, while the VWEI mean slope is ~0.049. At N=25 that yields Welch t ~= 5 (p ~ 1e-5), comfortably below alpha=0.01, with margin even at the worst-corner VWEI parameters (t ~= 4.3). The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame (common x distribution per subject) and on single-subject slices, so between_subject_variance is well-defined; degenerate cases (all-tie rows, zero x variance, constant y) return finite values rather than NaN.

This metric isolates the sharpest structural sign clash in the design. Ten of the 32 base pairs (trials 1-5, 8-9 and their A/B mirrors 17-21, 24-25; 30 observations per subject after 3 repetitions) have the property that the 95%-validity expert endorses one option and that same option carries strictly more total endorsements than its rival (which is either empty or carries only junk 50%-expert endorsements). On exactly these trials the two theories make opposite majority predictions with no parameter able to reverse the sign. VWEI: the v=.95 cue's weight logit(.95)^gamma (~25.5 at gamma=3, still the largest weight for any gamma in [2.8,3.2]) dominates every possible opposing coalition of cues 2-6, and 50%-expert endorsements carry exactly zero weight at every gamma, so P(follow top cue) sits at ~0.97-0.99 (sigmoid(0.205*25.5) with the small lapse). SDI: every endorsement adds a near-unit penalty (d_j in [0.93,0.98] for delta in [0,0.05]), and the top-cue option is always the endorsement-majority option here, so P(follow top cue) averages ~0.18 pre-lapse, ~0.22 after the epsilon lapse — i.e., the majority choice is the LESS-endorsed option. Expected gap ~0.75 (SDI ~0.22 vs VWEI ~0.98) with per-subject binomial standard error of only ~0.07 (30 trials, p near 0.2 or 0.98), so at N=25 the Welch t-test separates the theories by dozens of standard errors. The metric is a plain choice rate, so it is well defined both on the pooled DataFrame and on each single subject's slice, and it uses only scalar hashing of the response column (sequence columns are converted to arrays, never hashed). Unlike a slope estimate over the junk-endorsement gradient (which is noisy at 6 samples per cell), this is a simple proportion over 30 trials per subject, keeping between-subject variance tight. It is falsifiable in both directions: near-ceiling following of the top cue under endorsement-majority conflict refutes SDI; majority avoidance of the top cue refutes VWEI, which has no mechanism (at any gamma, since gamma only rescales positive log-odds weights) for preferring the option with fewer endorsements.

The design's double dissociation is exploited at its two strongest, sign-aligned points. COMPONENT 1 uses the count-matched big-validity-gap trials (pairs 6/18: a single 0.90 endorsement vs a single 0.60 endorsement, 8 trials per subject). Here VWEI's amplified log-odds weights produce P(follow the 0.90 expert) ≈ 0.84-0.94 across its entire (gamma, beta, epsilon) box, while SDI is pinned near chance (0.50-0.55) because its penalty difference at equal endorsement counts is driven only by delta ≤ 0.05 and alpha ≤ 0.05 — it is structurally near-blind to WHO endorses when counts match. COMPONENT 2 uses the ridge-crest conflict (pairs 10/22: four 0.75 experts vs one 0.80 expert, 8 trials per subject), scored +1 for choosing the coalition. VWEI's evidence sum favors the coalition (P ≈ 0.61-0.65 box-wide, since 4*w(0.75) > w(0.80) at gamma ≈ 3), while SDI's penalty difference of ~3 units at beta ≈ 1 drives P(coalition) ≈ 0.08-0.12 box-wide. Averaging the two aligned rates yields an expected pooled value of ~0.75 under VWEI vs ~0.31 under SDI — a ~0.44 mean gap. Between-subject variance is essentially binomial (each component uses 8 trials; var of the average ≈ 0.01 for both theories), so at N = 25 the Welch t-statistic is expected around 15 (p << 0.001). The metric is a plain choice rate on structurally identified trial cells (no theory fitting, no likelihood evaluation), works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on single-subject slices, avoids hashing any sequence-valued column, and degrades gracefully to 0.5 if a cell is somehow absent. Note the sign alignment is essential: both components are scored in the direction VWEI predicts (follow the strong expert; follow the weight-matched coalition), so the two gaps add rather than cancel.

The design's experts split cleanly into a high-validity group (features 0-6, validities 0.65-0.95) and a low-validity group (features 7-14, validity 0.60), and every trial pits a pure-high option against a pure-low option. This yields two orthogonal conflict families. FAMILY 1 (matched endorsement counts, 12 unique pairs, 48 trials/subject: e.g. one 0.95 endorser vs one 0.60 endorser; 2x0.90 vs 2x0.60): SDI's skepticism weight (1-v)^delta is nearly flat over the validity range (delta in [0, 0.05]), so its penalty difference is ~0 and its weak alpha tie-break pushes it slightly TOWARD the high-validity option (P ~ 0.51-0.55). VPS's penalty c0 + c1*v^kappa rises steeply in validity, so it systematically prefers the LOW-validity option (P(high) ~ 0.28 at mid parameters, and < 0.47 across its entire parameter box since D = c1*(v_lo^kappa - v_hi^kappa) < 0 structurally). FAMILY 2 (count conflicts where the FEWER-endorsed option is the high-validity one, 8 unique pairs, 32 trials/subject: 3x0.60 vs 2x0.90; 4x0.60 vs 3x0.90; 2x0.90 vs 3x0.60; 1x0.90 vs 2x0.60): SDI follows the endorsement count and picks the high-validity option with P ~ 0.70-0.73; VPS finds the low-validity majority cheaper per endorsement and picks the high-validity option only ~0.14-0.50 of the time (mean ~0.30). Cells where the fewer-endorsed option is the LOW-validity one (trials 9, 12, 21, 24) are agreed upon by both theories and are deliberately excluded so they cannot dilute the contrast. The metric averages P(choose the high-validity-group option) over the two families: SDI predicts ~0.62, VPS predicts ~0.29 — a gap of ~0.33 with per-subject standard deviation of only ~0.05 (binomial noise over 48 + 32 trials), giving a Welch t-statistic around 20 at N=25 (p << 0.001). The contrast is sign-robust across both theories' full parameter boxes: even at VPS's most SDI-like corner (c0=0.15, c1=0.7, kappa=1.6, beta=1.6, eps=0.13) the composite only rises to ~0.40, while SDI's least favorable corner stays ~0.59. The metric uses only the high/low validity grouping (threshold 0.65), which is invariant to the exact validities assigned to features 7-14, and it is well-defined both on the pooled DataFrame and on any single subject's 96-trial slice.

The design's Family 1 (pairs 1-6 and their mirrors 13-18) is a pure matched-count assay: both options carry exactly k endorsements, so every pure count term (SDI's near-uniform skepticism weights at delta near 0, and VPS's flat c0 term) cancels exactly, leaving only the validity-sensitive component. There the two theories make strictly opposite-sign predictions that are parameter-robust across their entire boxes: VPS prefers the LOWER-validity coalition (mid-parameter P ~ 0.69, 0.82, 0.89, 0.93, 0.87, 0.93 for k = 1..4 ladders; box floors still >= 0.60 and rising with k), while SDI is pinned at or below 0.50 on every matched-count pair (its validity sensitivity has the wrong sign and is bounded by ~0.064 + alpha*Delta-logit, giving ~0.42-0.48 at mid parameters). The metric therefore is simply the proportion of choices of the low-validity coalition over all matched-count trials, identified stimulus-side from the rating vectors and the fixed validity list (order randomization and A/B mirroring are handled automatically because the side is computed per trial from content, not position). Expected values: VPS ~0.85, SDI ~0.45 — a mean gap of ~0.40. Per subject this is a proportion over 48 Bernoulli trials (binomial SD ~0.05-0.07), and even adding parameter heterogeneity across the boxes the per-subject SD stays ~0.08-0.09 on each side, so at N=25 the Welch t-statistic is on the order of 15+, far beyond the alpha=0.01 threshold. The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame (canonical point estimate) and on each subject's slice (for the between-subject variance), and uses only scalar groupings (row iteration), avoiding any hashing of list-valued cells.

The design's actual validities are 0.50 (features 0-5) and 0.60 (features 6-19), so the entire DCD-vs-VPS dissociation lives on matched-endorsement-count trials: there the flat count term c0 cancels in BOTH theories and the choice is driven purely by the shape of the distrust weight near chance validity. VPS's penalty c0 + c1*v^kappa is strictly increasing in v, so on every matched-count pair it sign-robustly avoids the 0.60 experts (per-extra-0.60-endorsement decision contribution between -0.146 and -0.074 across its whole box, giving a weighted P(higher-validity side) around 0.38 at mid parameters, <= ~0.45 even at the most forgiving box corner). DCD's dampened charge c1*(2v-1)^kappa nearly vanishes at v=0.6 (0.022-0.043) and is actively opposed by the residual trust term alpha*logit(0.6) (0.032-0.049), so its matched-count decision variable stays within about +/-0.011 per endorsement and P(higher-validity side) stays at/above chance (~0.51 at mid, >= ~0.49 across the box). The metric is the m-weighted proportion of choosing the side with more 0.60-expert endorsements over all matched-count, non-tie trials (78 of 96 trials per subject; weights m = 1,2,3,4 concentrate on the cells with the largest predicted separation, e.g. m=4: DCD ~0.52 vs VPS ~0.31). It is a simple bounded proportion, so per-subject binomial noise is small (SD ~0.06 over 78 trials with these weights) and parameter heterogeneity barely moves DCD off 0.5 while VPS stays pinned below 0.45 — giving a mean gap of ~0.13 with tight per-subject values, far beyond what N=25 needs for a Welch t-test at alpha=0.01. Count-conflict trials (pairs 16/32) and pure validity ties (pairs 1/2/17/18) are excluded because both theories agree there, so including them would only add noise.

The metric is the proportion of trials on which the subject chose the option carrying MORE endorsements from the five v=0.50 (coin-flip) experts. Every one of the 24 unique pairs (96 trials/subject, 4 reps each) has a strict coin-flip asymmetry, so all trials contribute, and the metric is a simple Bernoulli proportion that works identically on the pooled data and on a single subject's 96-trial slice. It targets the single structural difference between the theories: VPS's raw-v charge c0+c1*v^kappa makes a 0.50 endorsement cost substantial distrust (exchange rate ~1.9 coin-flips per 0.75 endorsement), while DCD's dampened charge c0+c1*(2v-1)^kappa collapses to the floor c0 at v=0.50 with a trust refund (exchange rate ~1.3). Consequently, on every cell family the VPS subject is more coin-flip tolerant: composition cells (mixed {v_hi,0.50} vs homogeneous mid-validity) give VPS 0.53/0.56/0.59 (pairs 1-3, amplified) vs DCD 0.44/0.39/0.33 — opposite-signed majorities that no parameterization in either box can reverse; exchange cells (75-coalition vs k coin-flips) give VPS 0.75/0.62/0.47/0.32/0.60 vs DCD 0.59/0.44/0.30/0.20/0.34; calibration cells give VPS 0.73/0.86 vs DCD 0.65/0.76. Averaging over all 24 pairs: VPS mid-parameter value ≈ 0.59, DCD ≈ 0.45 — a 0.146 mean gap that is disjoint across the two theories' full parameter boxes (VPS per-cell box ranges stay above DCD's on essentially every cell, with the composition cells sign-robust). Per-subject standard deviation is ~0.05 (binomial over 96 trials) plus modest parameter heterogeneity (~0.02-0.04), giving Welch t ≈ 8-9 at N=25, far below alpha=0.01. Averaging over all cells (rather than only the sign-conflict cells) maximizes the standardized gap because the added trials shrink the binomial variance faster than the moderate cells dilute the mean difference, and it makes the metric a single interpretable behavioral quantity — coin-flip endorsement tolerance — rather than a hand-picked subset of trials.
